title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
summary: Support insert, remove and getRandom in average O(1). Keep values in an ArrayList (for random access) and a map from value to its index. To remove, move the last element into the removed slot and pop the end, so the list never has holes.
intuition: An array gives O(1) random picks; a map gives O(1) lookups.
Removing from the middle is O(n), so swap with the last element and remove the end instead.
Update the moved element's index in the map.
pitfalls: Forgetting to update the moved element's index.
Removing by index with `list.remove(int)` from the middle is O(n).
Using a HashSet alone: there's no O(1) random pick.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
summary: Store values per key with timestamps; get(key, t) returns the value with the largest timestamp ≤ t. Timestamps arrive in increasing order, so each key's list is already sorted: binary search it.

complexity.note: set is O(1) (append); get is a binary search.

intuition: Map each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs.
Strictly increasing timestamps keep each list sorted for free.
get = find the last timestamp ≤ t (an upper-bound search, minus one).
TreeMap.floorEntry is a one-line alternative.
pitfalls: Returning a value with a timestamp greater than t.

title: Snapshot Array
summary: An array that can take snapshots and read any index as of any snapshot. Copying the array on every snap is too slow. Instead, each index keeps a list of (snapId, value) changes; get binary-searches for the last change made at or before the requested snapshot.

complexity.note: set and snap are O(1); get is a binary search over that index's history.

intuition: Only store values that changed, tagged with the current snapshot id.
Several sets between snaps overwrite the same (snapId, value) entry.
get(index, id) = last entry with snapId ≤ id.
pitfalls: Copying the whole array on snap: O(n) per snap.
Off-by-one: snap returns the id of the snapshot just taken, then the counter increments.

title: Design Twitter
category: Design · K-way merge with a heap
summary: Post tweets, follow and unfollow, and get the 10 most recent tweets from yourself and the people you follow. Each user keeps their own tweets, newest last, with a global timestamp. The news feed merges those lists with a max-heap by time and stops after 10.

complexity.note: F = number of followees. post, follow and unfollow are O(1).

intuition: A global counter orders tweets across users.
The feed is a merge of sorted lists: push each user's newest tweet, pop the newest overall, push that user's next tweet.
Users always see their own tweets: include yourself in the merge.
Unfollowing yourself should do nothing.
pitfalls: Collecting every tweet and sorting is O(T log T) per feed.
Allowing a user to unfollow themselves.

title: Maximum Frequency Stack
summary: pop removes the most frequent element, breaking ties by recency. Keep each value's frequency and a stack for every frequency level. Pushing x with new frequency f puts it on stack f; popping takes from the highest non-empty level.
intuition: An element with frequency 3 sits on stacks 1, 2 and 3: one copy per level it reached.
The top of the highest stack is the most frequent and, among ties, the most recent.
After popping, decrease its frequency; if that stack empties, lower `maxFreq`.
pitfalls: A heap of (freq, time) works but is O(log n).
Forgetting to lower maxFreq when its stack becomes empty.

Python.code:
class FreqStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.freq = Counter()
        self.group = defaultdict(list)
        self.max_freq = 0

    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
        self.freq[x] += 1
        f = self.freq[x]
        self.max_freq = max(self.max_freq, f)
        self.group[f].append(x)

    def pop(self) -> int:
        x = self.group[self.max_freq].pop()
        self.freq[x] -= 1
        if not self.group[self.max_freq]: self.max_freq -= 1
        return x
